verses.zh: 耶和华又对约伯说：
verses.en: Then the Lord answered[NOTE:1] Job:
notes: See note at Job 38:1.

verses.zh: 强辩的岂可与全能者争论吗？与　神辩驳的可以回答这些吧！
verses.en: “Will the one who contends[NOTE:1] with the Almighty correct him?[NOTE:2] Let the person who accuses God give him an answer!”
notes: The form רֹב (rov) is the infinitive absolute from the verb רִיב (riv, “contend”). Dhorme wishes to repoint it to make it the active participle, the “one who argues with the Almighty.”

The verb יִסּוֹר (yissor) is found only here, but comes from a common root meaning “to correct; to reprove.” Several suggestions have been made to improve on the MT. Dhorme read it יָסוּר (yasur) in the sense of “to turn aside; to yield.” Ehrlich read this emendation as “to come to an end.” But the MT could be read as “to correct; to instruct.”

verses.zh: 于是，约伯回答耶和华说：
verses.en: Then Job answered the Lord:

verses.zh: 我是卑贱的！我用甚么回答你呢？只好用手捂口。
verses.en: “Indeed, I am completely unworthy[NOTE:1]—how could I reply to you?I put[NOTE:2] my hand over my mouth to silence myself.[NOTE:3]
notes: The word קַלֹּתִי (qalloti) means “to be light; to be of small account; to be unimportant.” From this comes the meaning “contemptible,” which in the causative stem would mean “to treat with contempt; to curse.” Dhorme tries to make the sentence a conditional clause and suggests this meaning: “If I have been thoughtless.” There is really no “if” in Job’s mind.
The perfect verb here should be classified as an instantaneous perfect; the action is simultaneous with the words.
The words “to silence myself” are supplied in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 我说了一次，再不回答；说了两次，就不再说。
verses.en: I have spoken once, but I cannot answer;twice, but I will say no more.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “I will not add.”

verses.zh: 于是，耶和华从旋风中回答约伯说：
verses.en: Then the Lord answered[NOTE:1] Job from the whirlwind:
notes: The speech can be divided into three parts: the invitation to Job to assume the throne and rule the world (40:7-14), the description of Behemoth (40:15-24), and the description of Leviathan (41:1-34).

verses.zh: 你要如勇士束腰；我问你，你可以指示我。
verses.en: “Get ready for a difficult task[NOTE:1] like a man. I will question you, and you will inform me.
notes: See note at Job 38:1.

verses.zh: 你岂可废弃我所拟定的？岂可定我有罪，好显自己为义吗？
verses.en: Would you indeed annul[NOTE:1] my justice?Would you declare me guilty so that you might be right?
notes: See note on “task” in 38:3.

verses.zh: 你有　神那样的膀臂吗？你能像他发雷声吗？
verses.en: Do you have an arm as powerful as God’s,[NOTE:1] and can you thunder with a voice like his?
notes: The verb פָּרַר (parar) means “to annul; to break; to frustrate.” It was one thing for Job to claim his own integrity, but it was another matter altogether to nullify God’s righteousness in the process.

verses.zh: 你要以荣耀庄严为妆饰，以尊荣威严为衣服；
verses.en: Adorn yourself, then, with majesty and excellency,and clothe yourself with glory and honor.

verses.zh: 要发出你满溢的怒气，见一切骄傲的人，使他降卑；
verses.en: Scatter abroad[NOTE:1] the abundance[NOTE:2] of your anger.Look at every proud man[NOTE:3] and bring him low.
notes: Heb “do you have an arm like God?” The words “as powerful as” have been supplied in the translation to clarify the metaphor.
The verb was used for scattering lightning (Job 37:11). God is challenging Job to unleash his power and judge wickedness in the world.
Heb “the overflowings.”

verses.zh: 见一切骄傲的人，将他制伏，把恶人践踏在本处；
verses.en: Look at every proud man and abase him;crush the wicked on the spot.[NOTE:1]
notes: The word was just used in the positive sense of excellence or majesty; now the exalted nature of the person refers to self-exaltation, or pride.

verses.zh: 将他们一同隐藏在尘土中，把他们的脸蒙蔽在隐密处；
verses.en: Hide them in the dust[NOTE:1] together;imprison[NOTE:2] them[NOTE:3] in the grave.[NOTE:4]
notes: The expression translated “on the spot” is the prepositional phrase תַּחְתָּם (takhtam, “under them”). “Under them” means in their place. But it can also mean “where someone stands, on the spot” (see Exod 16:29; Jos 6:5; Judg 7:21, etc.).
The word “dust” can mean “ground” here, or more likely, “grave.”
The verb חָבַשׁ (khavash) means “to bind.” In Arabic the word means “to bind” in the sense of “to imprison,” and that fits here.
Heb “their faces.”

verses.zh: 我就认你右手能以救自己。
verses.en: Then I myself will acknowledge[NOTE:1] to youthat your own right hand can save you.[NOTE:2]
notes: The word is “secret place,” the place where he is to hide them, i.e., the grave. The text uses the word “secret place” as a metonymy for the grave.
The verb is usually translated “praise,” but with the sense of a public declaration or acknowledgment. It is from יָדָה (yadah, in the Hiphil, as here, “give thanks, laud”).

verses.zh: 你且观看河马；我造你也造它。它吃草与牛一样；
verses.en: “Look now at Behemoth,[NOTE:1] which I made as[NOTE:2] I made you;it eats grass like the ox.
notes: The imperfect verb has the nuance of potential imperfect: “can save; is able to save.”

The next ten verses are devoted to a portrayal of Behemoth (the name means “beast” in Hebrew). It does not fit any of the present material very well, and so many think the section is a later addition. Its style is more like that of a textbook. Moreover, if the animal is a real animal (the usual suggestion is the hippopotamus), then the location of such an animal is Egypt and not Palestine. Some have identified these creatures Behemoth and Leviathan as mythological creatures (Gunkel, Pope). Others point out that these creatures could have been dinosaurs (P. J. Maarten, NIDOTTE, 2:780; H. M. Morris, The Remarkable Record of Job, 115-22). Most would say they are real animals, but probably mythologized by the pagans. So the pagan reader would receive an additional impact from this point about God’s sovereignty over all nature.

verses.zh: 它的气力在腰间，能力在肚腹的筋上。
verses.en: Look[NOTE:1] at its strength in its loinsand its power in the muscles of its belly.
notes: By form the word is the feminine plural of the Hebrew word for “beast.” Here it is an abstract word—a title.

verses.zh: 它摇动尾巴如香柏树；它大腿的筋互相联络。
verses.en: It makes its tail stiff[NOTE:1] like a cedar;the sinews of its thighs are tightly wound.
notes: Heb “with you.” The meaning could be temporal (“when I made you”)—perhaps a reference to the sixth day of creation (Gen 1:24).

verses.zh: 它的骨头好像铜管；它的肢体彷佛铁棍。
verses.en: Its bones are tubes of bronze,its limbs like bars of iron.

verses.zh: 它在　神所造的物中为首；创造它的给它刀剑。
verses.en: It ranks first among the works of God;[NOTE:1] the One who made it has furnished it with a sword.[NOTE:2]
notes: In both of these verses הִנֶּה (hinneh, “behold”) has the deictic force (the word is from Greek δείκνυμι, deiknumi, “to show”). It calls attention to something by pointing it out. The expression goes with the sudden look, the raised eye, the pointing hand—“O look!”

The verb חָפַץ (khafats) occurs only here. It may have the meaning “to make stiff; to make taut” (Arabic). The LXX and the Syriac versions support this with “erects.” But there is another Arabic word that could be cognate, meaning “arch, bend.” This would give the idea of the tail swaying. The other reading seems to make better sense here. However, “stiff” presents a serious problem with the view that the animal is the hippopotamus.

verses.zh: 诸山给它出食物，也是百兽游玩之处。
verses.en: For the hills bring it food,[NOTE:1] where all the wild animals play.
notes: Heb “the ways of God.”sn This may be a reference to Gen 1:24, where the first of the animal creation was the cattle—behemah (בְּהֵמָה).

verses.zh: 它伏在莲叶之下，卧在芦苇隐密处和水洼子里。
verses.en: Under the lotus trees it lies,in the secrecy of the reeds and the marsh.

verses.zh: 莲叶的阴凉遮蔽它；溪旁的柳树环绕它。
verses.en: The lotus trees conceal it in their[NOTE:1] shadow;the poplars by the stream conceal it.
notes: The literal reading of the MT is “let the one who made him draw near [with] his sword.” The sword is apparently a reference to the teeth or tusks of the animal, which cut vegetation like a sword. But the idea of a weapon is easier to see, and so the people who favor the mythological background see here a reference to God’s slaying the Beast. There are again many suggestions on how to read the line. The RV probably has the safest: “He that made him has furnished him with his sword” (the sword being a reference to the sharp tusks with which he can attack).

verses.zh: 河水泛滥，它不发战；就是约旦河的水涨到它口边，也是安然。
verses.en: If the river rages,[NOTE:1] it is not disturbed;it is secure,[NOTE:2] though the Jordan should surge up to its mouth.
notes: The word בּוּל (bul) probably refers to food. Many take it as an abbreviated form of יְבוּל (yevul, “produce of the field”). The vegetation that is produced on the low hills is what is meant.
The suffix is singular, but must refer to the trees’ shade.

verses.zh: 在它防备的时候，谁能捉拿它？谁能牢笼它穿它的鼻子呢？
verses.en: Can anyone catch it by its eyes[NOTE:1] or pierce its nose with a snare?[NOTE:2]
notes: The word ordinarily means “to oppress.” So many commentators have proposed suitable changes: “overflows” (Beer), “gushes” (Duhm), “swells violently” (Dhorme, from a word that means “be strong”).
Or “he remains calm.”
